title: Biological Warfare at the 1346 Siege of Caffa (quoting de' Mussi, Istoria de Morbo, catapult passage)
ask_addressed: Quote primary passages at their loci with composition date and basis, and the strongest scholarly caution on the Caffa story.
quote: lobbed into the city in the hope that the intolerable stench would kill everyone inside
summary: Quotes the Horrox translation of de' Mussi: dying besiegers had corpses placed in catapults and thrown into Caffa, after which the air and water were tainted. This is the only source for the catapult story.
limits: A single non-eyewitness narrative written 1348-49; translation is Horrox's as printed by Wheelis; Wheelis footnotes that these were technically trebuchets. The passage states the claim, it does not corroborate it.

strand.to: Genoese Caffa and, by ship, Italy
strand.what: plague (Yersinia pestis) said to be passed to Caffa by catapulted corpses, then to Italy by fleeing Christians; schema has no 'pathogen' category

text.work: Gabriele de' Mussi, Istoria de Morbo (Historia de morbo)
text.locator: opening narrative on Tana and the siege of Caffa (no chapter numbering given in the source)
text.edition: Horrox, R. (ed.), The Black Death (Manchester UP, 1994), English translation of the Latin, as quoted in Wheelis 2002 (EID 8(9))

composition.basis: Wheelis (2002) states the account 'is presumed to have been written in 1348 or early 1349'; Zanders (2021) says he probably wrote a few years after the plague reached Genoa and Piacenza (1347-48)

text.witness: Original lost; sole extant copy in a compilation c. 1367 (Wheelis 2002), found in Breslau/Wroclaw library and first published by Henschel 1842 (Zanders 2021)

title: Biological Warfare at the 1346 Siege of Caffa (quoting de' Mussi: 'what we ourselves have seen, or known, or consider likely')
ask_addressed: Quote primary passages at their loci with composition date and basis, and the strongest scholarly caution on the Caffa story.
quote: Now it is time that we passed from east to west to discuss all the things which we ourselves have seen
summary: De' Mussi himself marks a shift from reported eastern events to what he saw, knew or thought likely in the west; the Caffa section is therefore not presented as his own witness.
limits: Archival deeds place de' Mussi in Piacenza through the first half of 1346 (Tononi, via Wheelis). Quote ends before 'or known, or consider likely', which the page continues with.

title: Biological Warfare at the 1346 Siege of Caffa (Wheelis's assessment)
ask_addressed: Quote primary passages at their loci with composition date and basis, and the strongest scholarly caution on the Caffa story.
quote: His account of biological attack is plausible, consistent with the technology of the time
summary: Concludes, from published translations and secondary literature, that a deliberate plague attack at Caffa is plausible and the best explanation of plague entering the city, while noting de' Mussi wrongly has plague reach Italy directly.
limits: Plausibility argument, not corroboration; rests on one non-eyewitness text; no ancient-DNA or independent contemporary source. Author is a microbiologist writing on biological-weapons history.

strand.what: plague said to be introduced deliberately into besieged Caffa

title: de Mussi and the Siege of Caffa: Origin of a Biological Warfare Allegation (Historical Notes 1)
venue: The Trench, Historical Notes no. 1 (working paper)
discipline: History of chemical and biological warfare
ask_addressed: Quote primary passages at their loci with composition date and basis, and the strongest scholarly caution on the Caffa story.
quote: regarding events in Caffa, de Mussi was a secondary source, but absent other write-ups, his remains the only contemporaneous account
summary: Traces how the single de' Mussi text became central to the Caffa story, notes no contemporary document corroborates the deliberate catapulting, and says nobody established that the Mongols had trebuchets able to throw a body over the wall.
limits: Self-published working paper ('research in progress'), not peer reviewed; author states conclusions may be revised.

title: Catapulting Cadavers: A Medieval Practice of Biological Warfare? (Historical Notes 2)
venue: The Trench, Historical Notes no. 2 (working paper)
discipline: History of chemical and biological warfare
ask_addressed: Quote primary passages at their loci with composition date and basis, and the strongest scholarly caution on the Caffa story.
quote: establishing the plausibility of certain circumstances that might have enabled a certain event to take place still does not prove that the event happened
summary: Surveys other medieval cadaver-catapulting claims and concludes whole-carcass cases rest on single non-eyewitness sources and never recur; Caffa fits that pattern.
limits: Working paper, not peer reviewed; year taken from the file path (2022/04), not printed on the page text read.

title: Climate-driven changes in Mediterranean grain trade mitigated famine but introduced the Black Death to medieval Europe
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: import grain from the Mongols of the Golden Horde around the Sea of Azov in 1347 CE
summary: Argues a post-volcanic famine made Venice, Genoa and Pisa import Golden Horde grain in 1347, and that this grain trade brought plague to Mediterranean ports: a trade route in place of the siege story.
limits: Historical-climatic argument from documentary sources; presented as the best explanation, not proven; no pathogen DNA tied to the grain ships.

strand.to: Italian maritime republics and Mediterranean ports
strand.what: Yersinia pestis in grain cargo and ships, 1347

title: The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: our data support an early fourteenth-century source of the second plague pandemic in central Eurasia
summary: Ancient DNA from seven people in two Issyk-Kul cemeteries (tombstones dated 1338-1339 'pestilence') gives Y. pestis genomes ancestral to the Black Death diversification, pointing to a Tian Shan source.
limits: Small sample; shows where an ancestral strain was in 1338-39, not the route to the Black Sea or Europe.

strand.from: Issyk-Kul / Tian Shan region (Mongol-era Central Asia)
strand.what: Y. pestis lineage ancestral to Black Death strains

title: Phylogeography of the second plague pandemic revealed through analysis of historical Yersinia pestis genomes
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: Our data support an initial entry of the bacterium through eastern Europe, the absence of genetic diversity during the Black Death
summary: 34 ancient genomes from ten European sites support one entry of plague through eastern Europe and no diversity within the Black Death; the paper says the source and route remain hypothetical.
limits: Its own introduction states early western-Russian outbreak genomes were lacking; says nothing on Mongol agency.

strand.what: Y. pestis, single Black Death strain

title: Integrative approach using Yersinia pestis genomes to revisit the historical landscape of plague during the Medieval Period
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: possibly by means of fur trade routes, as well as the recirculation of plague within the human population
summary: Offers a rival route reading: repeated introductions into western ports, possibly along fur-trade routes, and links the Ibn al-Wardi 'Land of Darkness' phrase to those routes.
limits: Interpretive; text itself says the hypothesis is only 'possibly' supported; the page's date for arrival 'through Genoese galleys from Caffa' cites other work.

title: Ibn al-Wardi's Risalah al-Naba' 'an al-Waba' (Dols translation), on the origin of the plague
venue: Near Eastern Numismatics... Studies in Honor of George C. Miles (AUB), pp. 443-55
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: The plague frightened and killed. It began in the land of darkness.
summary: Contemporary Syrian eyewitness places the origin in the 'land of darkness' (Dols's note: 'northern Asia') and lists spread through China, India, Sind, Uzbek lands, Transoxiana, Persia, Crimea and Rum.
limits: 'Land of darkness' is vague; the list is a literary summary, not a dated route. Dols's footnote glosses it, Ibn al-Wardi does not.

strand.what: plague, described as spreading westward over about fifteen years

text.edition: Dols, M.W., 'Ibn al-Wardi's Risalah al-naba' 'an al-waba'', in Kouymjian (ed.), Near Eastern Numismatics... (AUB, 1974), 443-55

composition.basis: Dols: Ibn al-Wardi died at Aleppo 27 Dhu'l-Hijja 749 / 18 March 1349 and the risalah was written shortly before his death

text.witness: Dols consulted British Museum Or. MS 3053 and Dar al-Kutub MS 102 majami' (copied 1665) among others; the earliest witness is not established from the pages read

title: The Book of Ser Marco Polo, vol. 2 (Yule-Cordier): the Polos' mangonels at Saianfu
authors: Polo M.; Yule H. (ed.), Cordier H.
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: we have with us among our followers men who are able to construct mangonels which shall cast such great stones
summary: Polo says two men of his party, a German and a Nestorian Christian, built stone-throwing engines for Kublai at the siege of Saianfu: a claimed transfer of siege-engine knowledge into Mongol China.
limits: Yule's edition year (1903) is the Gutenberg edition's standard date, not read on the page. Polo's own narrative is dubious on chronology (see next candidate).

title: Plague and the Mongol conquest of Baghdad (1258)? A reevaluation of the sources
authors: Brack J., Biran M., Amitai R.
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: there is no evidence for the appearance of Plague during or immediately after the Mongol conquests in the Middle East
summary: Rereads Persian, Syriac and Arabic sources and finds no plague at Baghdad in 1258 and no Mongol transmission of it.

title: Plague history, Mongol history, and the processes of focalisation leading up to the Black Death: a response to Brack et al.
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: reconstruction of the biological processes of ‘focalisation’ is now the most urgent question in plague historiography
summary: Defends the view that plague circulated in western Asia in the 13th-14th centuries as an emerging zoonosis before the 1340s, whatever the exact 1258 timing.
limits: Authors are the targets of the critique above; a scenario, not a documented route.

title: Dangers of Noncritical Use of Historical Plague Data
ask_addressed: Mongol-era exchange and the Black Death: primary accounts, ancient-DNA studies of Yersinia pestis, and what is disputed about the route of the Black Death.
quote: noncritical use and reproduction of preexisting data sets can also limit our understanding of how infectious diseases evolved
